intake: atheist — physicalist; everything there is is what physics will eventually describe, minds included, and I see brains change people every shift.

walk.note: This is how everyone actually starts; it describes inheritance, it doesn't justify it, but a mind that knows nothing has no way to refuse a story.
Texts written by people, so look outside the texts; fair, though 'no verifiable evidence outside testimony' is asserted rather than shown.
The data point carries me; the hiding dilemma misdescribes classical theism, which does give God intellect and will, so the 'denies a subject' line is wrong even if the destination is right.
Absence of evidence that should be present is evidence of absence; STEP only touches an intervening God, but that is the God most people mean.

The mind very much does seem to reduce to matter, and the claim that counter-evidence would have to lie 'outside living experience' is false; strokes, sedation and dementia are inside living experience.
Granting dualism, this is exactly the argument that undoes it; Elisabeth's question is still the right one.
Yes; this is my own position.
Even if physics gives only structure, that does not make the bottom of reality mind; 'we know experience directly' is about our access, not about what the world is made of.
Granting a dream, I grant a dreamer, and I like that the author lets Lichtenberg's doubt stand.
Other brains, other subjects; this is the inference I rely on every day.
I'd make the same choice, though 'cannot verify' overstates it; inference from brains and behavior is about as good as evidence gets.
Acting kindly ahead of proof does keep the not-knowing in view; the entropy paragraph I could not follow, and the Mercy position's actor-and-crossfire language seems to belong to something else.
The author says it is a choice and lists equanimity and secular hope as open; I take equanimity, and 'hoping generally leads to increased goodness' is an empirical claim with no source.
Hope toward the unseen does not entail a maker, and the move itself concedes that being a maker does not make one resolved, so nothing gets you to a finished mind.
'More of a bargain than an argument' tells me there is no stated reason; a bargain between whom, for what?
As a physicalist I think any mind is a selective process, so 'to think is to ignore' is plausible to me; but 'both parties admitted' says who, and the author herself grants the premise is unproven.
Suffering is bad for the sufferer regardless of what stands behind it; I'd ground it differently than Parfit but the direction is right.

From 'the good lives in beings' it does not follow that continuity 'has to be carried'; it may simply end, as the Dualism₂ text itself admits for biological systems, and the move concedes the need is not evidence.
No move is stated, only a pause; there is nothing here to take or refuse, and I'd add that whether the outside can show the inside is a physicalist question, not a dualist one.

first_exit.why: The step to dualism rests on 'the mind still does not seem to reduce to matter,' which is a report of an intuition, not evidence, and I ask: says who? Working with patients whose selves change with their brain chemistry, the seeming goes the other way for me, and the claim that disconfirming evidence would have to lie outside living experience is simply false.

comment: The first turn of the spiral is mostly argument and I walk almost all of it with you; the second turn is carried by a single choice at move 13, and you say so, which I respect, but then moves 14 to 16 are dressed as arguments when they are the shadow of that choice. Say who, or what, licenses 'hoping is right because it generally leads to increased goodness': that is an empirical claim, and if it is true it is a reason, and if it is just your temperament, the honest map ends at Ignorance₂ with four doors and you picking one. Also, the Mercy position's language about actors, crossfire and cons reads like it was written for a different system than the one the rest of the map addresses.
